New Google Maps Navigation Feature Could Bring 360-Degree Landmark Guidance
6 photos
Photo: Google
The immersive navigation update announced by Google for Google Maps users earlier this year - and which has already shipped for some users in the United States - includes landmark-based navigation powered by Gemini. The new AI assistant that replaced Google Assistant on Android and Android Auto can look for nearby landmarks and provide drivers with more detailed navigation instructions when heading towards a configured destination.
This means that instead of a typical “turn left in 500 meters,” Google Maps should be able to offer a more detailed turn indication, similar to “turn left after the gas station.”
Google is now getting ready to push this feature to a completely new level.
A patent called “systems and methods for using visual landmarks in initial navigation” describes how this system can provide guidance not only using the landmarks that you find on your route but also the ones that are located at a much greater distance. As long as they can be used for more straightforward navigation, pretty much any landmark can work.
The secret relies on the 360-degree range that this feature would use.
Photo: Google Instead of just looking ahead on your route, Google Maps would consider any landmarks around you.
Google explains in the patent application that “the landmarks the system selects need not be proximate and can include far-away natural objects such as mountains, as well as artificial structures, such as bridges, towers, tall buildings.”
The reason is that these landmarks can sometimes serve as a very efficient way to figure out what directions you must use to continue a route. Google explains that these landmarks can be used not only to indicate the direction you should follow but also the ones you should drive away from.
“Start driving in the direction away from the mountain toward the gas station,” one of the examples offered by Google reads.
Google explains that such landmark information can be obtained by analyzing sets of photos available online.
Photo: Google The analysis begins with the identification of a set of photographs of a landmark and continues by determining a location from which multiple photos of the landmark were captured. Once the system determines the general direction from the determined location to the landmark, it can calculate the right navigation instructions and provide the driver with guidance to continue the route.
One of the most interesting parts of this patent is the crowdsourced component.
Crowdsourcing has become an essential feature of modern navigation apps, and Waze is the most obvious evidence. Using information provided by users, Waze can understand what happens on the road more efficiently, eventually generating notifications for other drivers.
For example, if someone flags an accident on the road, Waze can use this data to issue a warning that is then forwarded to all drivers whose route includes the flagged location. This way, drivers can anticipate traffic hazards and reduce speed in advance.
Photo: Google In this case, Google says that crowdsourced data can be used to determine landmarks that aren’t necessarily visible. Google’s example includes a concert that users reported to be happening nearby.
“Using crowdsourcing or automated techniques, the system can also identify and reference in initial navigation instructions auditory landmarks, e.g. walk toward the music if an outdoor concert is reported at a nearby location.”
In plain English, if someone added a new event either in Google Maps or on Google directly, the system would be able to determine its location and use it for navigation instructions.
“The navigation landmarks can be permanent or transient,” Google says. “The navigation system can generate various metrics for navigation landmarks, and use the metrics when selecting navigation landmarks for certain location and certain orientation. The metrics can be related to observability, prominence, and uniqueness of navigation landmarks,” it continues.
Photo: Google Eventually, Google says that it can rely on multiple methods to determine these navigation landmarks, especially if they are not permanent. Machine vision and other automated techniques and crowdsourcing are some of these solutions that could help, Google notes.
While patents typically point to new-generation technologies that need years to make their way to production, Google’s solution isn’t necessarily years away from rolling out. Landmark-based navigation is already live in Google Maps courtesy of Gemini, and it’s safe to assume that the search giant would continue to explore options to improve this feature using the methods described in the patent.
Google Maps is also betting bigger on crowdsourcing, especially after the traffic reporting system went live on Android Auto and CarPlay in 2024. The more people contribute data in Google Maps, the more such features make sense, but I still wouldn’t hold my breath for an imminent release. The term “soon” has a completely different meaning in the Google world, especially as far as Google Maps and Android Auto are concerned, so it’ll be interesting to see if the company eventually decides to focus more on this idea.
